text: Sommer made his living as a lithographer and painted on his own time. He started as an apprentice in Detroit, where he was born, and later studied in Munich for a year. In 1907 he moved to Cleveland to work for Otis Lithograph, and there he helped found the Kokoon Arts Club, a bohemian group that met to paint, talk and drink. Offset printing took his job in 1929. After that he showed at the Whitney Biennial and the Museum of Modern Art. He liked farm scenes and young children.

Astrup failed his Latin exams because he was busy drawing, and that ended his father's plan to make him a priest. Born on the island of Frøya, he grew up in Jølster, where he lived and painted for most of his life. He studied in Oslo and Paris, then in Berlin under Lovis Corinth. His farm landscapes of western Norway use bold, strong colour, and people compare them with Munch's work. He also made woodcuts. Tuberculosis and asthma wore him down, and he died of pneumonia at 47.

Lockwood de Forest began as a landscape painter and became a designer of Indian-style interiors. As a young man he studied with Frederic Edwin Church, who was his mentor. His honeymoon in British India lasted two years. There he met a philanthropist in Ahmadabad, and together they opened a woodcarving workshop that supplied carved furniture and architectural woodwork to Tiffany's firm Associated Artists. He then ran his own decorating business for thirty years. After he retired he moved to Santa Barbara and went back to painting.

Francia's real name was Raibolini, and he made his living as a goldsmith and medallist in Bologna. He also directed the city mint. His earliest known painting, the Felicini Madonna, is dated 1494. He ran a large workshop, where Marcantonio Raimondi first learned to engrave. A story says Raphael's Santa Cecilia left him so depressed that he died of it. Historians now discard that tale, since the two men were friends.

Horthemels engraved copper plates in Paris for nearly fifty years and signed more than sixty of them. Her first published work, in 1707, was a frontispiece for Lesage's novel Le Diable boiteux. Engraving ran in the family. Her sister Marie-Anne-Hyacinthe married the engraver Nicolas-Henri Tardieu, and in 1713 she herself married the engraver Charles-Nicolas Cochin the Elder. Later plates carry her married name, Cochin. Their son became engraver to the court of Louis XV, and she died at his house in Paris.

Dietrich could imitate almost any old master, and that was both his talent and his trouble. At eighteen he finished a painting in two hours, and Augustus II of Saxony paid for him to study in Italy and the Netherlands. Winckelmann called him the Raphael of landscape. Some of his Rembrandt-style pictures in Dresden carry fake dates and Rembrandt's name. In 1741 he became court painter there, on condition that he deliver four cabinet pictures a year. He never developed a style of his own.

Raphael became Perugino's most famous pupil. Perugino himself came from Città della Pieve, and his nickname only says that he worked in Perugia. Scholars still argue about whether his family was poor or rich, and nobody knows his exact birth date. Vasari says he trained in Verrocchio's workshop next to Leonardo. About 1480 Pope Sixtus IV called him to Rome to paint frescoes on the Sistine Chapel walls. He was also one of the first central Italian painters to work in oil.

Medicine came first for Carus, and painting second. In 1814 he became professor of obstetrics in Dresden, and in the same years he taught himself oil painting while working under Caspar David Friedrich. He also wrote on art theory. His own idea of landscape painting was to show the inner workings of the earth, and he called it Erdlebenbildkunst. Goethe was his friend. In 1844 he travelled through Britain as personal physician to the King of Saxony, and Queen Victoria hosted them at Windsor Castle.

Lemoyne taught both Natoire and François Boucher. He won the Prix de Rome in 1711 and went to Italy to study, and later he became a professor at the Académie and first painter to Louis XV. His rival for the title of leading painter of his generation was Jean-François de Troy. Contemporaries called Lemoyne the new Le Brun, and he did much of his best work at Versailles. He killed himself in 1737, at the height of his career.

Neumann grew up very poor, but Veit Hanns Schnorr von Carolsfeld liked his work and took him on as a student at the Academy of Fine Arts. His father worked as a colorist and his brother became a wood engraver. Neumann later worked in the studio of the copper engraver Henry Winkles. Many of his portraits were printed in Die Gartenlaube and the Illustrirte Zeitung. He was best known for portraits of musicians, including Franz Schubert and Robert Franz.

Elias Martin's carpenter father wanted his son in the trade, but the boy preferred art and became an apprentice to a Swedish court painter. A job designing ship ornaments led him to Augustin Ehrensvärd, who took him to the sea fortress of Sveaborg for two years. In 1766 Martin went to Paris and tried to copy Boucher, but the style did not suit him. He moved on to London. Nationalencyklopedin calls him Sweden's first great landscape painter.

Vereshchagin graduated first in his class at the naval school and then left the service right away to study drawing. In Paris he studied under Gérôme, though he disagreed with his methods. In 1867 he joined a Russian army expedition to Central Asia. His courage at the siege of Samarkand won him the Cross of St. George. As a war artist he painted realist scenes so graphic that many were never printed or shown to the public.

Hardly anything is known about Correggio's early life. His real name was Antonio Allegri, and his birth date is a guess of about 1489. He was probably apprenticed in Modena, where he would have met the work of Francesco Francia. Dynamic compositions and steep foreshortening made him an early sign of the Baroque. He is considered a master of chiaroscuro. Correggio led the Parma school of the High Renaissance.

Nothing is known for certain about Van der Goes before 1467, when he became a master in the painters' guild of Ghent. Some historians guess that Dieric Bouts was his teacher, but there is no evidence. He painted the Adoration of the Magi, now in Berlin, and worked on an altarpiece ordered by the banker Tommaso Portinari. That Portinari Altarpiece reached Florence in 1483, after the painter had already died. It helped shape realism and the use of colour in Italian Renaissance art.

Davies trained as a lawyer and ended up making the Norfolk Broads famous. He was the eldest child of a geologist. In 1871, just after qualifying, he read an account of the Broads and applied to join a law practice in Norwich. He became a prolific photographer and writer there. His books include The Swan and Her Crew, which follows three young naturalists and sportsmen through the Broads and rivers of Norfolk.

Born in Belgium, Haes became one of the three grand masters of Spanish landscape painting. In 1857 he was named the first professor of landscape painting at the Royal Academy of San Fernando in Madrid. He was the first in Spain to teach painting straight from nature. His pupil Aureliano de Beruete became a landscape master too. In 1876 the Spanish state bought his view of the Canal of Mancorbo in the Picos de Europa for the Prado.

A goldsmith's son and one of nine children, Parreiras left the Imperial Academy in Rio after two years to study with the German immigrant Georg Grimm. In 1886 Emperor Pedro II bought one of his works. That let him go back to formal study and sail to Europe, where he trained in Venice under Filippo Carcano. Home again, he taught landscape painting and followed Grimm by taking his students outdoors to paint. After disagreements over the curriculum, he opened a school of his own, the Escola do Ar Livre.

Lam Qua painted Western-style portraits mostly for Western clients, and he was the first Chinese portrait painter shown in the West. His workshop stood in New China Street among the Thirteen Factories in Canton. Some contemporaries said he studied with George Chinnery, though Chinnery denied it. Lam Qua charged less than Chinnery. From 1836 to 1855 he painted patients of Peter Parker, an American medical missionary who ordered pictures of people with large tumors before their operations. Some of those paintings are now at Yale.

Monkeys made Mori Sosen famous. Robert van Gulik called him an undisputed master of painting the Japanese macaque. He also painted deer, boars and peafowl. When the Dutch brought a gibbon to Japan in 1809, nobody there had seen a live one for centuries, and Mori made a picture record of the event. Nobody knows whether he was born in Osaka, Nagasaki or Nishinomiya, but he lived in Osaka most of his life.

Sesson came from the Satake clan, but his father disinherited him and he became a Zen monk at Shōsō-ji temple. He took the character for snow in his name from Sesshū, whom he admired, though some scholars doubt that Sesshū shaped his painting. In Ibaraki he is called "Sesshū of the west, Sesson of the east". He painted landscapes such as Eight Views of Xiaoxiang and legendary figures like Li Tieguai. Twice he went to Aizu to teach painting to the daimyō Ashina Moriuji.

Vogel got his first training from his father, the portrait painter Christian Leberecht Vogel. As a young man in Dresden he taught the children of Baron von Löwenstern, who then invited him to Livonia. In 1808 he moved on to Saint Petersburg, opened a studio and painted nobles and diplomats so successfully that he grew rich. The money paid for a long-wanted grand tour of Italy. He ended up living in Rome until 1820, among the many German artists working there.

Gaul painted soldiers and the American West. He studied at the National Academy of Design in New York and visited the West in 1876. To add to his income he illustrated for Century Magazine while it ran Civil War memoirs, and three of his paintings became frontispieces for Battles and Leaders of the Civil War. In 1882 he was elected a full academician for Charging the Battery, the youngest person ever given that honor. He later won medals in Paris, Chicago and Buffalo.

Antwerp-born but raised in Dordrecht, Wolffort trained there and joined the local Guild of Saint Luke in 1603. Around 1615 he went back to Antwerp to work in the studio of Otto van Veen, one of Rubens's teachers, and he lived in van Veen's house. He painted mostly religious and mythological history scenes. His workshop probably turned out copies of his works. Two of his pupils, Pieter van Lint and Pieter van Mol, worked there for a while as copyists.

Garrard came from a family of artists that traced its descent to Marcus Gheeraerts the Younger, painter to Queen Elizabeth I. He studied with Joseph Simpson and then with Sawrey Gilpin, and he entered the Royal Academy in 1778. Joshua Reynolds noticed his View of a Brewhouse Yard and ordered a similar picture. In 1795 Garrard had the idea that plaster models of cattle would be useful to landscape painters. Later he lobbied Parliament to protect the copyright of modellers.

Fouquet may have invented the portrait miniature. He was born in Tours, and little is known about his early training. Sometime in the 1440s he went to Italy, the first French artist to do so, and the work of Fra Angelico and Filarete left a mark on him. During the 1450s he began working for the French court, where Charles VII and later Louis XI were among his patrons. He painted panels as well as manuscript illuminations.

Bellotti trained in Venice under Girolamo Forabosco and became known for portraits and character heads. Orlandi says he worked for Cardinal Mazzarino and for Cardinal Ottoboni, who later became Pope Alexander VIII. In Mantua he was superintendent of the Gonzaga galleries and villas. After wandering from court to court, he went back to Lake Garda. He died poor in Gargnano in 1700.

Dong Yuan held an official post under the Southern Tang dynasty and painted alongside it. He studied the styles of Li Sixun and Wang Wei, then added more sophisticated perspective. With his pupil Juran he founded the Southern style of Chinese landscape painting, called the Jiangnan style. Jing Hao and Guan Tong of the Northern style complete the group of four seminal painters of that time. The standard for brush painting in China for the next nine centuries came from his elegant manner.

Prendergast and his twin sister, Lucy, were born at their family's trading post in St. John's, Newfoundland. After it failed the family moved to Boston, where he was apprenticed to a commercial artist. At 14 he took a job wrapping packages in a dry goods store, and that work is said to have shaped his taste for bright, flat patterns. His landscapes and scenes of modern life have mosaic-like colour. He belonged to The Eight, a group of American artists who otherwise stood for the Ashcan School.

Amsterdam was where Arnoud van Halen was born and where he died. Houbraken says he painted the portrait of Christoffel Pierson for the Panpoeticon Batavum, a cabinet of poets that held portraits of over 100 people by 1712. The RKD says he was also called Arend or Aquila van Halen. He is known for portraits, engravings and book titlepages. Houbraken wrote about him in the early 1700s.

A furrier's son from Lyon, Révoil got a proper education even though his family needed him at home. In 1793 poverty forced them to send him to a manufacturer of patriotic wallpapers. Two years later he found a place in the studio of Jacques-Louis David. He began with Greek vase paintings and scenes of the Revolution, then turned almost entirely to medieval history. People later called that manner the Troubadour Style. They didn't mean it kindly.

Latour had his first lessons at home from his mother, Marie Simons, a miniaturist herself. He later trained with Louis-Marie Autissier in Brussels and with Jean-Baptiste Augustin in Paris. King William I made him official miniaturist to the House of Orange. Belgium became a kingdom in 1831, and he kept a similar post under the new monarchy. He could paint accurate portraits from memory. His pupils included his own son Édouard, who painted genre scenes.

Cole grew up in the smoke of industrial Britain, and his paintings show the American wilderness as its opposite. Born in Bolton le Moors, he moved with his family to Steubenville, Ohio, in 1818. He founded the Hudson River School. His romantic landscapes often put small figures or buildings against moody nature. They also criticise industry, cities and the push westward.

Vibert came from a family of engravers and a famous rose breeder. His maternal grandfather, the engraver Jean-Pierre-Marie Jazet, taught him young. He cared more for painting than engraving, so he entered the École des Beaux-Arts at sixteen and stayed six years. His Salon debut in 1863 showed La Sieste and Repentir. During the Franco-Prussian War he served as a sharpshooter and was wounded at the battle of Malmaison. The Legion of Honour followed.

Shunkō is generally credited with designing the first large-head actor portraits, called ōkubi-e. He studied under Katsukawa Shunshō, possibly as the master's first pupil, and signed with the same small jar-shaped seal. His earliest known work is a book illustration from 1766, and from about 1771 he made actor prints. At 45 he became partly paralysed and stopped designing prints. He kept painting with his left hand.

Many paintings of dead game once credited to Jan Baptist Weenix are now given to his son Jan. Jan trained with his father, together with his cousin Melchior d'Hondecoeter. His father died young in 1659, and by twenty the son was said to match him in breadth of treatment and richness of colour. Nobody knows his exact birth date, because the baptismal record of his Catholic church didn't survive. A marriage notice of 1679 says he was born in Amsterdam.

La Touche's whole formal art training was ten years of drawing lessons from a local instructor at three francs a month. The Franco-Prussian War ended them, when his family went back to Normandy for safety. Even so, in 1875 he made his Salon debut with a bas-relief portrait medallion of the actor Got and several etchings. Within a few years he was meeting Degas and Manet at the Café de la Nouvelle Athènes. There he was introduced to Zola.

The youngest of six children of a rich Catholic who owned the De Werelt brewery in Haarlem, Soutman was a contemporary of Frans Hals. Houbraken says he trained with Rubens in Antwerp. Rubens probably recommended him as an excellent painter when Prince Władysław Vasa visited Antwerp in 1624. That same year Soutman went to Poland and became royal court painter. He served King Sigismund III Vasa until 1628, then returned to Haarlem.

Louis XIV called Charles Le Brun the greatest French artist of all time. Chancellor Séguier noticed the Paris boy and put him in Simon Vouet's studio at eleven. At fifteen he was already getting commissions from Cardinal Richelieu. In 1642 he left for Rome with Nicolas Poussin. He stayed four years on a pension from the chancellor, working under Poussin and taking over the older painter's theories of art.

After 1843 Bodmer began signing his work K Bodmer, probably because his son Charles-Henry Barbizon had just been born. In Germany he was well known for watercolours and aquatints of the Rhine, Mosel and Lahn. After an expedition to the American West he moved to France and joined the Barbizon School. There he painted animals and landscapes in oil. He illustrated books too. In 1877 he became a Knight of the Legion of Honour.

Gilpin's brother Sawrey became a full-time painter, but William chose the church. He kept sketching all the same, and he helped originate the idea of the picturesque. Unusually for his time, he liked wild and rugged mountain scenery. In 1748 he anonymously published a part guidebook, part essay on the gardens at Stowe. As headmaster of Cheam School he fined boys instead of beating them, and he let them keep gardens and run small shops.

Hunt's middle name came from a clerk's mistake. He was born William Hobman Hunt, and when he found the misspelling he adopted Holman. The Royal Academy art schools rejected him at first. In 1848, after meeting Dante Gabriel Rossetti, he started the Pre-Raphaelite movement with John Everett Millais. Hunt stayed truest to its ideals for his whole career, even after his wife Fanny Waugh died in childbirth in Italy at the end of 1866. He sculpted her tomb himself.

Savoldo was highly regarded in his own lifetime, then slipped from memory, and the art trade sold many of his works as Giorgione's. Only about 40 paintings by him are known, six of them portraits, plus a handful of drawings. He worked mostly in Venice and was also called Girolamo da Brescia. He is noted for subtle colour, chiaroscuro and sober realism. Some of his portraits look like extracts from larger narratives. Interest in his work revived in the 19th century.

Novelli trained with the Venetian painter Jacopo Amigoni and was accepted into the academy in Venice in 1768. He painted altarpieces and frescoes across northern Italy, and some of his commissions came from Catherine the Great. Around 1779 he moved to Rome, where he stayed more than twenty years. He then went back to Venice and died there. His memoirs were not published until 1834.

Swan first studied in Worcester and Lambeth and at the Royal Academy Schools, then in Paris with Jean-Léon Gérôme and Emmanuel Frémiet. His picture The Prodigal Son, bought for the Chantrey collection in 1889, made his reputation, and it is now in Tate Britain. His younger sister Alice and his wife Mary Rankin Swan were both artists, and their daughter Mary Alice became a sculptor. He became a Royal Academician in 1905.

His father's will told Brodowski to study mathematics, and at first he did. Art lessons with Marcello Bacciarelli ran alongside. In Paris he tutored a politician's children while studying with the miniaturist Jean-Baptiste Augustin, and later he took lessons from Jacques-Louis David on a government stipend. He balked at the rule that he must send paintings home for approval, and the money stopped in 1812. He stayed in Paris and lived on portraits, with François Gérard as his teacher and patron.

Rimmer's father believed he was the French dauphin, the son of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, and that belief troubled the son. Born in Liverpool, William grew up in Boston, where he learned shoemaking. At fifteen he became a draughtsman and sign-painter, and later he worked for a lithographer. In 1841 he toured New England painting portraits. After studying with a respected physician he also practiced medicine for about twelve years.

Pratt went to England to escort his cousin, who was marrying the American painter Benjamin West, and he ended up staying two and a half years as West's pupil and colleague. There he painted The American School, one of his best known works. He had trained from 1745 with his uncle, the painter James Claypoole, and learned the business side of portraiture too. Back in America in 1768 he became famous for portraits of American men and women.

Sánchez Cotán painted still lifes in an austere style, more so than similar works in the Netherlands and Italy. He was born in Orgaz near Toledo, and he was a friend and perhaps pupil of Blas de Prado, whose mannerist style with touches of realism he developed further. For about twenty years he worked in Toledo for aristocratic patrons, painting altarpieces, portraits and still lifes. Educated intellectuals there liked the pictures. His best-known still lifes date from around the start of the seventeenth century.

Ten children were too many for Milani to support in Bologna, so he moved to Rome. He had trained in Bologna under Cesare Gennari and Lorenzo Pasinelli, though his style came from the Carracci. In Rome the commissions abounded, among them a Beheaded St. John the Baptist for the church of the Bergamaschi. For many years he taught there too. His pupils included Giuseppe Marchesi, called il Sansone, and Antonio Gionima.

Roberts earned the nickname Bulldog for his tenacity and drive. Born in Dorset, he came to Melbourne as a boy, worked as a photographer's assistant and studied art at night under Louis Buvelot. He returned to England for the Royal Academy Schools, and in 1885 he helped found the Box Hill artists' camp with Frederick McCubbin. With Arthur Streeton and Charles Conder he staged the 9 by 5 Impression Exhibition, Australia's first avant-garde art show. He made his living painting society portraits. In 1903 he finished The Big Picture, the best-known image of the first Australian Parliament.

Maurice Dumont published his poems under the name Jean Stels. They appeared in L'Art libre, a satirical paper he founded and illustrated himself. In Paris he trained as an engraver and took classes with Léon Bonnat. His review L'Épreuve printed more than a hundred original prints by sixty artists, among them Maurice Denis, Gauguin, Bonnard and Vuillard. In 1895 he joined Paul Fort to relaunch the review Le Livre d'art. He died young, in Avranches.

Blomstedt began by studying law in Helsinki, and he took drawing lessons at the same time. His earliest paintings were decorative and symbolist. In the 1890s he went to Paris with Pekka Halonen and joined the Académie Julian. He is said to have studied with Paul Gauguin during several stays. He also gathered material for a Finnish textbook on painting technique and colour chemistry. For the Finnish pavilion at the 1900 Paris World's Fair he painted three panels, and he won a bronze medal.

Hardly anything is recorded about Kolb's life, though some of his engraved views of buildings and cities are well known. In 1838 he lived in Nuremberg and showed work at the city museum. His birth date is unknown. He also worked in Johann Poppel's graphic studio in Munich. Many of the prints made there were copied from drawings by the painter Johann Friedrich Lange. Kolb's view of Cologne Cathedral includes the railway and road bridge finished in 1859.

A violinist's son from Modena, Niccolò dell'Abbate trained in the studio of the sculptor Antonio Begarelli, alongside Alberto Fontana. His specialty was long friezes with secular and mythological subjects. For the counts Boiardo he painted twelve frescoes in the Rocca di Scandiano, and he portrayed the counts themselves in the late 1530s. Later he joined the School of Fontainebleau, the group of artists who brought the Italian Renaissance to France.

Vasconi grew up in Rome, where his grandfather Carlo Fontana and his uncle Francesco taught him the basics of architecture. After his uncle died in 1708 he left for Venice. There he engraved illustrations for architecture books, among them Vignola's rules for the five orders and Palladio's Four Books. Back in Rome in 1716, he anonymously published a book of his own architectural studies. Later he engraved Filippo Juvarra's designs for Palazzo Madama and the twin churches of Santa Cristina and San Carlo in Turin.

Aigner commanded the Academic Legion in Vienna during the 1848 revolutions, and he was court-martialed for high treason and condemned to death. Prince Windisch-Grätz pardoned him. He had studied under Friedrich von Amerling and Carl Rahl, and he painted portraits of Franz Joseph, Empress Elisabeth, the poet Nikolaus Lenau and the playwright Franz Grillparzer. According to Ripley's Believe It or Not, a Capuchin friar whose name he never knew saved his life three times. The same friar presided over his funeral in 1886.

Titian came from Pieve di Cadore, a small town near Belluno. His real name was Tiziano Vecellio. His career was successful from the start. Patrons came first from Venice and its possessions, then from the north Italian princes, and finally from the Habsburgs and the papacy. He was equally good at portraits, landscape backgrounds, and mythological and religious subjects. Along with Giorgione he is considered a founder of the Venetian school.

Leonardo called Salaì a liar, a thief, stubborn and a glutton, and Salaì stole from him at least five times. Leonardo kept him in his household for more than twenty-five years anyway. His real name was Gian Giacomo Caprotti, and he came to Leonardo at ten, the son of a tenant on Leonardo's vineyard near Milan. He modelled for Leonardo's St. John the Baptist and Bacchus. He also painted on his own, under the name Andrea Salaì.

Only nine paintings can be firmly attributed to Fra Carnevale, and most of those have been disputed at some point. He is also cited as Bartolomeo di Giovanni Corradini. He was a pupil of Antonio Alberti and later worked in Filippo Lippi's studio in Florence. Before 1450 he returned to Urbino and joined the Dominican house of San Domenico. Farquhar claims he taught Giovanni Santi.

Born without arms and with only vestigial legs, Biffin wrote and painted with her mouth. She was apprenticed to Emmanuel Dukes, who showed her as an attraction throughout England. At St. Bartholomew's Fair in 1808 she caught the eye of the Earl of Morton, who paid for lessons from the Royal Academy painter William Craig. In 1821 the Society of Arts gave her a medal for a historical miniature. The royal family commissioned miniature portraits from her.

Raffaëlli had only three months of formal training, under Gérôme in 1871. He came to painting from music and theatre, and he also acted and wrote. Until 1876 he painted mostly costume pictures. Then he turned to the people of his own time, especially peasants, workers and ragpickers seen in the suburbs of Paris. Critics such as Huysmans championed the new work, and so did Edgar Degas. He showed with the Impressionists.

Le Sidaner settled at Gerberoy in Picardy and painted there for over thirty years. He built gardens in the ruins of the medieval fortress, and his views of them show tables just left by diners, dappled in sunlight under roses. Before that he travelled widely in France and Europe. He liked nuanced greys and opals, laid on in uneven dappled strokes. He was also a skilled painter of nocturnes.

Gillot is best known as the teacher of Watteau and Lancret. Watteau was his apprentice from 1703 to 1708. In 1715 his playful mythological landscapes, Feast of Pan and Feast of Bacchus, got him into the Academy of Painting in Paris. He then adapted to fashionable taste and brought in decorative fêtes champêtres, though his pupils soon surpassed him at them. Commedia dell'arte characters fill his paintings, a taste he passed on to Watteau. He also designed scenery and costumes for the opera and theatre.

Wright grew up on the family manor at Haminalahti near Kuopio, the youngest of nine surviving children, and he was taught at home. His ancestors were Scottish merchants who had settled in Narva in the 17th century. Two older brothers, Magnus and Wilhelm, also became painters and illustrators. He learned to look hard at nature while hunting and exploring. He is best known for landscapes and animal paintings, above all his detailed birds.

Millais was eleven when he became the youngest student ever to enter the Royal Academy Schools. The Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood was founded at his family's home on Gower Street in London. His Christ in the House of His Parents stirred up a lot of controversy, and he painted Ophelia in 1851 and 1852. By the mid-1850s he was moving away from the Pre-Raphaelite style toward a new kind of realism. His later pictures sold so well that he became one of the wealthiest artists of his day.

Panini's most famous pictures include the interior of the Pantheon, painted for Francesco Algarotti, and his views of picture galleries hung with scenes of Rome. He was born in Piacenza and trained there under Giuseppe Natali and Andrea Galluzzi. Later he worked in Rome, where he took a particular interest in the city's antiquities. Most of his ruin pictures carry fanciful embellishments in the capriccio tradition, much like those of Marco Ricci. He also painted a portrait of Pope Benedict XIV.

Born Christian Emil Marie Küpper in Utrecht, the son of a photographer, he took his name from his stepfather, Theodorus Doesburg. He always regarded his stepfather as his natural father, so his first works are signed Theo Doesburg. The van came later. After a short period of training in acting and singing, he decided to become a storekeeper. He is best known as the founder and leader of De Stijl. He married three times.

The house in Speyer where Feuerbach was born is now a small museum. His father was an archaeologist. After the Düsseldorf Academy and then Munich, he left in 1850 with other dissatisfied students for the academy at Antwerp. In Paris he studied under Thomas Couture and painted his first major work, Hafiz at the Fountain, in 1852. In 1854 the Grand Duke of Baden paid for a trip to Venice.

Tan'yū was appointed the shogunate's first official painter in 1617, and prestigious commissions followed. He was the grandson of Kanō Eitoku, and his given name was Morinobu. In the 1620s and 1630s he made large works for Edo Castle, Nijō Castle and the shrine at Nikkō Tōshō-gū. They are screens and panels of natural subjects such as tigers and birds, in bright colour and plenty of gold leaf. Many of the best-known Kanō works today are by him.

Crivelli came from a family of painters in Venice. He is said to have studied under Jacobello del Fiore, who was still painting in 1436, when Crivelli was probably only a boy. Details of his career are thin. He left the Veneto by 1458 and spent most of the rest of his life in the March of Ancona. There he developed a personal style very unlike that of his Venetian contemporary Giovanni Bellini, keeping a conservative Late Gothic taste for decoration.

Filippino's parents had both broken vows of celibacy. After his birth they received a papal dispensation to marry, arranged by Lorenzo de' Medici, but Vasari says they never did. His father was the painter Fra Filippo Lippi, and Filippino first trained in his workshop. Florence was his main base, though he worked in Rome from 1488 and later around Milan and in Bologna. Most of his pictures are religious subjects, with a few portraits and classical scenes.

Pieter van der Werff learned to paint from his older brother Adriaen and assisted him. The RKD says he spent most of his life in Rotterdam, painting the rich and famous. Two portraits of about 1709 in the Victoria Art Gallery in Bath hint that he may have gone to England to look for commissions. He is also the first recorded painter to use the pigment Prussian blue, in a copy of his brother's painting.

Carpaccio studied under Gentile Bellini and is often compared with him. What set him apart was his command of perspective, his close attention to architectural detail and his bold colour. Antonello da Messina and Early Netherlandish painting influenced him. In Saint Augustine in His Study, from 1502, the room is full of exotic objects, the kind collectors wanted at the time. He worked on everything from single canvases to altarpieces and large picture cycles.

Vanderlyn's grandfather Pieter was also a painter. Young John worked for a print seller in New York, then copied Gilbert Stuart's portraits in Philadelphia, among them one of Aaron Burr. Burr took him on as a protégé and in 1796 sent him to Paris, where he studied for five years. In 1801 he came home and lived in Burr's house while Burr was vice president under Thomas Jefferson. He painted portraits of Burr and his daughter.

The son of a sculptor and furniture manufacturer, Danhauser took his first painting lessons from his father. He later studied with Johann Peter Krafft and held his first exhibition in 1826. The patriarch of Venice, Johann Ladislaus Pyrker, invited him to Venice, where he began to study the Italian masters. His moralising pictures owe a clear debt to William Hogarth. Few people appreciated them in his time. He is counted among the Biedermeier artists, along with Waldmüller and Fendi.

Grottger died at thirty, cut short by an incurable illness, but he was still one of the most prominent Polish artists of the mid 19th century. His father was a Polish officer of German origin who commanded a regiment of Uhlans in the failed November Uprising against Russia. At eleven Artur was sent to Lwów to apprentice with Jan Kanty Maszkowski, and he briefly studied with Juliusz Kossak. In 1852 he went on to Kraków.

Teniers was court painter and curator to Archduke Leopold Wilhelm, the art-loving governor of the Habsburg Netherlands, and he made a printed catalogue of the Archduke's collection. He also painted pictures of collections, along with peasants, tavern scenes and alchemists. He founded the Antwerp Academy, where young artists learned to draw and sculpt in the hope of reviving Flemish art. He was extremely versatile and prolific. Today he is remembered as the leading Flemish genre painter of his day.

Three major seventeenth-century art writers, Félibien, Sandrart and De Piles, ignored Ochtervelt, even though he painted a great deal. Houbraken was the first to mention him, calling him a pupil of Berchem at the same time as Pieter de Hooch. He added a remark about weak perspective in interior scenes, and it isn't clear whether he meant Hooch or Ochtervelt. Later Van der Aa said his style was closer to Gerard Terborch. Vermeer and De Hooch were among his contemporaries.

The first Netherlandish painter to think of himself mainly as a landscape painter was Joachim Patinir. He came from Wallonia but worked in Antwerp, then the centre of the art market in the Low Countries. He effectively invented the world landscape, a panoramic northern Renaissance style. Albrecht Dürer was his friend, and so was Quentin Metsys, who added the figures to their joint Temptation of St Anthony, now in the Prado. Patinir died in 1524.

Schuch wanted to paint heads "like still-lifes, tone by tone, without emotion". He was born in Vienna but lived mostly in Germany, Italy and France. While based in Paris in the 1880s and early 1890s he admired Monet, whom he called the Rembrandt of plein-air painting, but Rembrandt himself and the Barbizon painters attracted him more. In the Netherlands in the summers of 1884 and 1885 he studied the old masters and filled notebooks with detailed descriptions of the colours he saw. Still lifes and landscapes were his main subjects.

Born Nils Johan Olsson, he took the name Blommér in Paris, after his home village of Blommeröd. He started as an apprentice to Magnus Körner in Lund. In 1839 he enrolled at the Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts. A generous scholarship in 1847 took him to Paris to study with Léon Cogniet. Swedish folk songs and the folklore motifs of Moritz von Schwind inspired him. He firmly believed nature had a soul.

Julius Goltzius's aunt Mayken Verhulst became the mother-in-law of Pieter Bruegel the Elder. His father, Hubert Goltzius, was a painter, printer and humanist. Julius began engraving in 1575, with plates after drawings by his elder brother Scipio for the father's books on coins. From 1577 he engraved for Plantin. Publishers in Antwerp and Cologne hired him regularly, often for exiled Flemish artists. He probably died in Antwerp well after 1601.

Barry painted a six-part series, The Progress of Human Culture, for the Great Room of the Royal Society of Arts in London. He insisted on making art by his own principles instead of his patrons', which makes him one of the earliest romantic painters in Britain. Born in Cork to a builder, he became professor of painting at the Royal Academy schools in 1782. His belligerent temper didn't help his reputation. Few people rated him until a Tate Gallery exhibition in 1983 led to a reassessment. William Blake was strongly influenced by him.

Van Loo learned painting from his father, Jean-Baptiste, in Turin and Rome. He then spent five years in Rome with his uncle Charles-André. In 1736 he became court painter to Philip V of Spain, and he was a founder-member of the Royal Academy of San Fernando in Madrid. He went back to Paris in 1753 and painted many portraits of Louis XV. He also painted the Portuguese statesman the Marquis of Pombal.

Serov is generally considered the main portraitist of his generation in Russia. His father was the composer Alexander Serov and his mother, Valentina, also composed, so he grew up in a highly artistic household. As a child he studied with Ilya Repin in Paris and Moscow, and later under Pavel Chistyakov at the St. Petersburg Academy. Friendships with Mikhail Vrubel and Konstantin Korovin shaped him. He was also closely tied to the Abramtsevo Colony.

Goshun founded the Shijō school of painting. Born into a wealthy family of mint officials, he was the oldest of six children. His parents had him tutored from an early age in classical history and literature, calligraphy, painting and poetry. Yosa Buson taught him literati painting and haiku. He wasn't an immediate success as a painter. He is sometimes called Matsumura Gekkei.

Żmurko took his first drawing lessons as a young boy in Lviv with the painter Franciszek Tepa. As a teenager he moved to Kraków, where Jan Matejko taught him at the Academy of Fine Arts. In Vienna he was accepted at the academy but soon left to study under Alexander von Wagner in Munich. He spent a short time in St. Petersburg too. Later he settled in Warsaw and stayed there until he died.

Neuhuys went to the municipal drawing school in Utrecht and then worked for a lithographer, until the firm went bankrupt. After that he devoted himself to drawing and painting. A royal stipend paid for lessons at the Antwerp Academy, where he painted interiors in the manner of Pieter de Hooch and specialised in the shine of satin clothes. In Amsterdam he met Jozef Israëls, Anton Mauve and the brothers Jacob and Matthijs Maris. When he moved to The Hague in 1876, his detailed manner loosened into a much freer stroke.

Savage began as a goldsmith and engraver, and he seemingly had no training as a painter. A portrait of George Washington brought him attention in 1790. He went to London to study under Benjamin West, then to Italy, and in 1794 he came back to run a picture gallery and art museum on Water Street in New York. He is best known for The Washington Family, a large group portrait he finished in 1796. It shows George and Martha Washington, two of her grandchildren and an enslaved servant, probably Christopher Sheels. He completed Congress Voting Independence too.

Huet painted singeries, scenes of monkeys, for the château de Chantilly, and Edmond de Goncourt long gave them to Watteau. The son of a goldsmith who painted on the side, he was best known as an animal painter. In 1733 he worked with Claude III Audran on the decoration of the château d'Anet for the Duchess of Maine. A painted harpsichord for the château de Thoiry is also attributed to him. His early work is hard to tell apart from that of his nephew Jean-Baptiste.

Linati set up the first lithographic press in Mexico. He co-founded and edited El Iris, a periodical that ran the first political cartoons in the country, and his activism got him forced out. Born into a noble family near Parma, he joined the Society of Engravers there at seventeen and later studied under Jacques-Louis David in Paris. He also took part in revolutionary causes in Italy and Spain. His best-known work is a hand-colored book of costumes of the people of Mexico.

Quinet ran a photo studio on the rue Cadet in Paris from about 1868 to 1882. Earlier he went to Algeria as assistant to the photographer Félix-Jacques Moulin, his father's brother-in-law. His portraits include the polar explorers Otto Torell and Julius von Payer and the British explorer Verney Lovett Cameron. At the second international congress of geographers he photographed the main events and every exhibition room, and he put the pictures in an album. His younger brother Achille patented a stereoscopic camera.

Buysse was meant to run his father's cotton mills, so he was sent to spinning mills in Germany and England to learn the trade. He painted in his spare time, took lessons from Louis Tytgadt and visited museums. His friend Émile Claus gave him plenty of advice and urged him to exhibit, which he began doing in 1894, at first only abroad. A degenerative illness from 1899 limited his travel. In 1900 he moved to Wondelgem, into a house by the Art Nouveau architect Paul Hankar, with a view of the Ghent-Terneuzen canal.

Erbslöh's father worked in New York for an export firm, and that is where Adolf was born. The family returned to Barmen in 1887. He trained for business although he could draw, and the year after his father died he dropped it to attend the academy in Karlsruhe. In 1905 he went on to Munich. In 1907 he married his second cousin Adeline Schuchard. The next year he came up with the plan for the Neue Künstlervereinigung München, and he was one of its founders.

Strobel's biggest painting, the Feast of Herod with the Beheading of St John the Baptist, is in the Prado. It looks like a religious subject but shows a lavish court banquet of his own time, with portraits of many leading figures of Central Europe. Nobody has been able to identify them all. Strobel came from Silesia, worked in Prague, and then moved to Poland to escape the Thirty Years War. There he painted portraits and religious works for the ruling elites and religious orders.

Bazzani spent most of his life in Mantua, a declining provincial city, yet he absorbed influences from far beyond it. Tortured poses sometimes recall expressionism. Fetti, Bencovich, Rubens and Magnasco are all said to have influenced him. A goldsmith's son, he apprenticed with the Parma painter Giovanni Canti. In 1752 he joined the faculty of the Mantua academy, and in 1767 he became its director.

Miller was one of the principal engravers of Turner. His pupil James Giles remembered that Miller's admiration for Turner was unbounded and that the pupils soon caught it. Miller's first published engraving, in 1814, was of an apple tree. He later moved to Hackney to work in George Cooke's workshop, where he drew plants from a neighbouring nursery. His last work illustrated Thomas Hood.
